noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know that metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between metal ions and the delocalised electrons
be able to use the models in 3.20 and 3.21 to interpret simple properties of metals, including electrical conductivity and high melting temperature

primer.text: Metals pool their outer-shell electrons into a delocalised sea that binds an array of positive ions from every direction. One model explains everything: conduction, heat transfer, malleable layer-sliding, high melting points, and why alloys jam the layers stronger. This note builds the electron-sea model and then reads the property table off it.

lessons.title: The sea that binds the metal
lessons.opening: In a metallic lattice, atoms pack tightly together and their outer-shell electrons detach to roam the whole structure as delocalised electrons. The abandoned atoms become positive ions that would repel each other - except that the surrounding electron sea pulls on every ion from every side, and it is that ion-to-sea attraction which holds the lattice stable.
keyPoints: Metal atoms pack tightly together in lattice structures.
Outer-shell electrons free to move throughout the structure are called delocalised electrons.
Once electrons delocalise, the metal atoms become positive ions.
The positive ions repel each other electrostatically.
The strong attraction between positive metal centres and the electron sea holds the lattice together.

low.restatement: Metal atoms drop their outer electrons into a shared pool; what remains are positive ions, and their grip on the pool - not on each other - is the metallic bond.
low.analogy: Swimmers leave their deck chairs (atoms become ions) and share one pool (electron sea); the chairs stay in place because everyone holds the pool's edge.
low.examPointer: Say the attraction is between positive ions and delocalised electrons - 'between the metal atoms' is the mark-losing phrasing.

medium.restatement: Delocalisation converts the crystal into an array of cations suspended in a mobile electron fluid: ion-ion repulsion exists but is overwhelmed by ion-electron attraction operating in all directions, which is why the structure coheres without any directional bond.
medium.analogy: Corks bobbing on shared water: corks push each other apart, yet each is held down by its grip on the water beneath.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the lattice does not blow apart, answer with the net attraction to the sea overruling ion-ion repulsion.

options.text: Outer-shell electrons free to move throughout the metal structure
options.explanation: They are not bound to any single atom.

options.text: Electrons locked into covalent bonds between atoms
options.explanation: Metallic bonding has no localised shared pairs.

options.text: Inner-shell electrons orbiting tightly
options.explanation: Delocalisation involves the outer shell only.

options.text: Free neutrons drifting between atoms
options.explanation: Neutrons stay in the nucleus.

check.stem: What charge do the metal centres carry after their electrons delocalise?

options.text: Positive - the atoms become positive ions
options.explanation: Losing electron grip leaves a net positive core.

options.text: Negative - they gain the shared electrons
options.explanation: The electrons are shared by all; each centre is positive.

options.text: Neutral - nothing changes for the atoms
options.explanation: Delocalisation is precisely the change.

options.text: Alternating positive and negative
options.explanation: Every metal centre is positive.

check.stem: Why does the lattice hold together despite ion-ion repulsion?

options.text: Attraction between each positive ion and the surrounding electron sea outweighs the repulsion
options.explanation: The sea pulls on every ion from all directions.

options.text: The ions actually attract each other directly
options.explanation: Like charges repel; the sea mediates the cohesion.

options.text: Repulsion vanishes inside metals
options.explanation: The repulsion exists but is overruled.

options.text: Neutrons cushion the ions apart
options.explanation: Neutrons are inside nuclei and play no binding role.

check.stem: Which statement about delocalised electrons is correct?

options.text: They are not bound to any particular atom
options.explanation: Belonging to the whole lattice is their defining trait.

options.text: They orbit fixed parent atoms
options.explanation: Delocalised means released from parentage.

options.text: They carry no charge
options.explanation: Their charge is exactly what mediates metallic bonding.

options.text: They only exist at the metal's surface
options.explanation: They roam the whole structure.

check.stem: A textbook diagram shows metal cations suspended in a shared electron pool. The bond holding each cation in place is

options.text: the electrostatic attraction between the cation and the delocalised electrons
options.explanation: That ion-to-sea pull is the metallic bond.

options.text: a covalent bond to its nearest neighbour
options.explanation: No fixed pairs exist in a metal.

options.text: an ionic bond to a nearby anion
options.explanation: No anions are present in a pure metal.

options.text: gravity between the heavy cores
options.explanation: Gravity is negligible at this scale.

check.modelAnswer: Delocalised electrons are outer-shell electrons free to move throughout the metal structure, not bound to their original atom.

check.stem: State what holds the metallic lattice together.
check.modelAnswer: What holds the lattice together is the strong electrostatic pull between positive metal ions and the surrounding delocalised-electron sea.

check.stem: Explain why metal atoms become positive ions when their electrons delocalise.
check.modelAnswer: The atoms' outer-shell electrons leave to roam the whole lattice, so each atomic centre is left with more protons than locally bound electrons - a net positive charge - even though the crystal overall stays neutral.

check.stem: Describe, in drawing terms, a correct exam sketch of metallic bonding in copper.
check.modelAnswer: Draw rows of labelled Cu+ ions in tight layers surrounded by a labelled sea of delocalised electrons filling the gaps - and note that the electron labels are what many sketches forget.

lessons.title: Properties forged by the sea
lessons.opening: The delocalised sea explains every headline property of a metal: high melting and boiling points from strong ion-to-sea attractions, electrical and thermal conduction from mobile charge carriers, and malleability from ion layers that slide without breaking the bonding. Alloys trade some of that slide for strength, and bonding strength itself rises with more sea electrons per atom, higher ionic charge and smaller ions.
keyPoints: Metal ions pack in hexagonal layers or cubic arrangements inside the giant lattice.
High melting and boiling points follow from the strong electrostatic ion-to-sea attractions.
Metals conduct electricity and heat because delocalised electrons move and carry energy.
Layers of ions slide without breaking the bonding, making metals malleable and ductile.
Alloying atoms block the sliding layers, so alloys outstrength pure metals.

low.restatement: One shared electron pool answers everything: it grips hard (high melting points), it flows (conduction), and it lets layers slip without snapping the grip (malleability).
low.analogy: A hall of standing dominoes on shared ball bearings: strong overall grip, easy local rearrangement, and something rolling through moves things along.
low.examPointer: Pair each property with its sea-based reason - the table of property-against-reason is the answer scaffold examiners expect.

medium.restatement: Metallic properties reduce to the mobility and strength of one interaction: charge and heat ride on electron mobility, melting resistance scales with ion-to-sea attraction, and layer-gliding malleability survives because the sea re-binds each shifted layer instantly - alloying atoms jam the glide planes and stiffen the whole array.
medium.analogy: A well-greased gear train: strong mounts (attraction), free rotation (conduction), and gear teeth that re-engage after slipping (malleability) - until grit (alloy atoms) jams the train stronger.
medium.examPointer: For alloy questions, state the jamming mechanism: foreign atoms of different size disrupt the regular layers and stop easy sliding.

check.stem: Why do metals have high melting and boiling points?

options.text: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons needs large energy to overcome
options.explanation: The ion-to-sea bonding runs through the whole giant lattice.

options.text: Covalent bonds between atoms must break
options.explanation: No directional covalent bonds exist in a metal lattice.

options.text: The electron sea insulates the ions from heat
options.explanation: Conduction, not insulation, is the electron behaviour.

options.text: Ions cannot vibrate at high temperature
options.explanation: Ion vibration is exactly what melting entails.

options.text: Delocalised electrons move through the structure carrying charge
options.explanation: Electrons entering one end displace others from the far end, so current flows.

options.text: Ions migrate between electrodes
options.explanation: The ions are fixed in the lattice; only electrons move.

options.text: Heat vibrations carry the current
options.explanation: Vibrations transfer heat, not charge.

options.text: Protons flow along the wires
options.explanation: Protons stay bound in nuclei.

options.text: Ion layers slide over one another while the electron sea maintains the attraction
options.explanation: The bonding survives the shift because the sea belongs to no particular atom.

options.text: Covalent bonds stretch and reform
options.explanation: No directional bonds exist to stretch.

options.text: Ions swap places with electrons
options.explanation: Ions keep their sites; layers glide instead.

options.text: The lattice shatters and reseals
options.explanation: Shattering is brittleness - the opposite property.

check.stem: Why is an alloy stronger than its pure parent metal?

options.text: Added atoms of different size disrupt the layers and block easy sliding
options.explanation: Irregular layers jam the glide that makes pure metals soft.

options.text: Alloying removes delocalised electrons entirely
options.explanation: The sea remains; it is the layer structure that is disrupted.

options.text: Alloying introduces ionic bonds
options.explanation: The bonding stays metallic.

options.text: Alloying melts and refreezes the metal stronger
options.explanation: No refreezing mechanism is involved.

check.stem: Which change strengthens the metallic bonding in a metal?

options.text: Increasing the number of delocalised electrons per atom
options.explanation: More sea electrons deepen the ion-to-sea attraction.

options.text: Increasing the size of the metal ions
options.explanation: Larger ions weaken the per-contact pull.

options.text: Decreasing the positive charge on the centres
options.explanation: Lower charge weakens attraction.

options.text: Widening the gaps between ions
options.explanation: Distance weakens electrostatic attraction.

check.stem: State the two packing arrangements metal ions commonly adopt in lattices.
check.modelAnswer: Metal ions commonly adopt hexagonal layer packing or a cubic packing plan.

check.stem: State the three changes that increase the strength of metallic attraction.
check.modelAnswer: More delocalised electrons per atom, higher positive charges on the metal centres, and smaller metal ions.

check.stem: Explain why metals conduct heat as well as electricity.
check.modelAnswer: The same mobile delocalised electrons that carry charge also transport kinetic energy: speeding electrons collide with metal atoms and ions, passing thermal energy along, alongside the increased vibration of the particles themselves.

check.stem: A jeweller wants a strong, shapeable gold ring. Explain why pure gold is chosen over a heavily alloyed wire for malleability, using the layer-sliding model.
check.modelAnswer: Pure gold's uniform layers glide under the hammer while the electron sea re-binds each shifted layer, so the metal shapes without cracking; heavy alloying would jam those glide planes, strengthening the piece but costing workability.

glossary.definition: The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the surrounding sea of delocalised electrons.
A tightly packed, layered or cubic array of metal ions held by the shared electron sea.
A metal structure with other atoms added, whose irregular layers block sliding and so strengthen the material.
